title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI, it's rewriting the org as if it didn't exist
dek: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads get the bonus pool and the right to divide it, and to hire you first have to prove AI can't do the job.
why: The founder of a 12-year hardware company explains the concrete mechanics of an org rewrite: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and with the pitfalls.
who: Founders, HR leaders and business owners pushing an AI org transformation, especially at hardware or consumer electronics companies where you want to move the org but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the small talk and the outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the org doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone has to use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the old organization and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of one person starting a company to redesign the roles and the process. So this is not accelerating the existing process, it's tearing the process down first and rebuilding it. He admits this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

points.h: The HARO lead comes from tech, not from HR
points.body: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT: the lead has to understand the business, and the person chosen is an old partner who started the company with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR lead leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a technology-oriented person runs it, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will do Agent Builder work) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people in the short term
points.body: Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an Agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line, sort out supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover it; short term two kinds of people must work together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead people from the business put 30% to 50% of their energy into AI-ification while still doing the business. The company also set up AI levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI navigators’ and above that ‘pilots’.

points.h: Circles erase functional power; the circle lead gets the bonus pool
points.body: Lockin's circles differ from project teams and from Huawei's matrix: a matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team around an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, the circle lead decides how to divide it, and can even decide how much to give himself; HR and the functional departments only have the right to advise. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates, and the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within six months to a year of the change the front line gets to decide first.

points.h: Experience can turn into a burden
points.body: Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear about doing things, and use it more than the old hands. His words are ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the most troublesome are the half-baked — whose experience hasn't arrived but who feel they are very experienced and can't change. Old hands have framework thinking and systematic thinking as their foundation, but which processes and which roles can be removed is easier for a clear-headed person to judge. The threshold for an AI management trainee is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring the ability to use skills and build Agents; only L3 can write workflows.

points.h: R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits the speed of transformation varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, because writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and a bigger bonus. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not raise quality, and that 60-point output doesn't stick around. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether the content can bring conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, then sit down again
points.body: Lockin ran three rounds of internal sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as the company-level twenty-odd Agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after the circles were formed, such as an Agent Builder for content marketing; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they are good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting minutes and the talk for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may finally be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results are very good.

points.h: To hire, you first have to prove AI can't do it
points.body: After a circle picks off people from the original department, if the boss wants to add headcount there are logically only two channels: find an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If you really must hire again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain clearly why a management trainee won't do and why AI won't do. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They will hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, doing the AI-native transformation together with Chen Bin.

points.h: IPD is not overturned, only accelerated
points.body: Chen Bin says inside the company he is in fact the most radical one, and people often pull him back and ask him to be more cautious. On deposits like Huawei's IPD, his judgment is: AI can only remake processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, from strategy to execution, SP to BP, used to take three months to half a year, now two months, doubling efficiency, but the nodes like the five looks and three settings are still there, just three weeks become three days. Training a product line manager used to take 10 to 15 years, now three to five years, but the rotations that should happen cannot be skipped.

points.h: Not every company should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three kinds of bosses — milk tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, and you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature and then choose, with lower trial-and-error cost. But the more frontier the tech company, the earlier it should embrace AI, because technology changes a lot and the market changes fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically mentions that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and the like should be cautious and not move first; milk tea shops are driven more by channels and operations, and AI can quickly build a feedback loop from the user end to the supply chain end, so it matters more there.

quotes.text: I think a native organization probably starts from AI first — whatever AI can do, as far as possible don't let a person do it. Think AI-native first, think about this thing, and even this process, as something that logically should be rebuilt.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm end-to-end, a small team around a value loop, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or the boundaries — make the functional power smaller, make the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Actually sometimes experience instead becomes a burden. It's better to have it, but the half-baked ones are the scary ones — their experience hasn't arrived, but they feel they're already very experienced, right? Can't change.

As far as possible we fill it with AI, right? Prioritize using AI — whatever AI can fill, AI fills. Unless it can't be filled, and if it can't be filled, then internally we say: either you say you'll find an AI management trainee to fill it, or you use more AI tokens.

It used to take at least three months to half a year; now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least double the efficiency. But the process itself hasn't changed, it's just that where I used to hold five meetings, it becomes three meetings, two meetings.

Actually look at the real value AI brings in this industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it brings, indeed a bit lower. And if it's lower, then you can, so to speak, wait until these — like us, the ones digging the pit and playing around, right? Or like Doubao, Volcano Engine, the ones doing it better — and then choose. That's fine.
